text: The following question stood in the name of  Mr Leong Mun Wai –   3 To ask the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance whether there is a net increase in the past reserves when state land is first sold and the sales proceeds are transferred to the financial assets, and when the land is sold again after reverting to the Government’s ownership upon the expiry of its lease.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Pritam Singh, would you like to move the question?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It has been explained before, but it bears repeating and some elaboration.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Under our land laws, which trace back to English land laws, all title to land in Singapore is derived from the state.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is from this ultimate title to land that is held by the state that interest in land, such as leases, can be carved out and granted by the state to other persons.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The leases confer ownership and possession of those lands to such other persons, but only for the duration of the lease.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The state retains the interest in the balance of the lands not leased, and for lands which have been leased, in the rest of the period not granted.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In the case where the state has granted a portion of its interests – for example, under a 99-year lease – to other persons, the state holds the remainder of those interests, meaning, after the 99th year for perpetuity – which we refer to as the “reversionary interests”.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Where the state has not granted any interest in a piece of land, or no one is named as the person owning the lease, that land remains “state land”.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: When we sell state land, we convert the physical asset into a financial asset.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, if we sell a parcel of state land at its fair market value of, say, $1 million, we no longer have the land for the term of the lease sold, but we have $1 million.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: After this transaction, there is no net increase in the reserves.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have merely changed the physical land in our reserves into an equivalent amount of financial reserves.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There is no new value created and hence, no addition to the reserves.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Let us see what happens to the cash and to the land.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The rest of the actual returns – that is, 100% of the actual returns minus 50% of the long-term expected real returns – is re-invested.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This rule strikes a balance between the needs of current and future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It preserves the real value of our reserves and assures us of a rainy-day fund in the event of future crises.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Let us turn to the land that has been sold.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As the state holds ultimate title to the land, the land automatically reverts to the state once the 99 years is up.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It then becomes state land again and will be protected as past reserves once again.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: When that happens, there is no net increase in our reserves either.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is because the reversionary interest in that parcel of land had all along formed part of our reserves.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In other words, the financial proceeds that we had earlier received was to make up for the state's loss of use of the land for 99 years, and not for the state giving the land away forever.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If the Government then carves out another lease of the same land and sells this land on a fresh lease, the same process as before will apply.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is just a conversion of one asset form to another.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: (b) There is no net increase in the reserves when land returns to the state after the lease expires, as the value of the lease did not include the value of the reversionary interest.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: (c) There is again, no increase in the reserves when the land which was returned to the Government is sold again.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As before, that is merely a conversion of one form of asset to another.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: (d) There is an increase in reserves when the Government invests and grows the financial assets.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is the outcome of careful and prudent management of our reserves by this Government and should not be taken for granted.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I move on to Mr Leong's second query.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There is no "triple payment" by Singaporeans for the land used to develop HDB flats.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: From time to time, the Government may need to compulsorily acquire land for public housing.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First, the Government will acquire the land and compensate the landowner for its value.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Since 2007, the compensation is based on fair market value.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This compensation may be funded from past reserves or Government revenues.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Land acquisition through SERS, for instance, is funded by past reserves.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Second, HDB will purchase the land from Government.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: HDB pays fair market value for it, just like any other buyer of state land.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Why do we not simply transfer the land to HDB at zero cost since it is a transaction between Government and a Government agency?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The reason is because, the transfer to HDB for developing public housing results in the land being taken out of the past reserves.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If fair market value is not paid in exchange for the land, the past reserves would be depleted.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There would be no corresponding financial asset to replace the physical asset and no land sale proceeds to invest and generate returns for use in the form of the NIRC.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Requiring HDB to pay fair market value for the land cost thus preserves the value of our past reserves for the benefit of all Singaporeans, both present and future.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The third transaction is when HDB sells flats to Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: HDB does so at a discount from fair market value to keep flat prices affordable.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The difference between the fair market value and HDB's posted price is the market subsidy.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In addition, the Government provides generous grants to eligible applicants, to purchase flats below HDB's posted price.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Because of these grants and subsidies, HDB's effective selling price is typically much lower than the total cost of development, which results in a revenue shortfall.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This shortfall is covered by a Government grant to HDB which is funded by NIRC and taxes, which are paid not only by Singaporeans but also by PRs, foreigners working and living in Singapore, tourists and companies and other tax-paying entities.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The answer to Mr Leong's second question, therefore, is that: (a) The Government does not profit from the sale of state land developed into public housing.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: (b) There is no triple payment by Singaporeans for state land used for public housing.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: (d) This can be seen from the fact that a private property of similar size and in a similar location would cost significantly more and also the fact that after the Minimum Occupation Period, HDB flat owners are typically able to sell their flats at comparable or higher prices than they paid when they purchased their flats from HDB.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The POFMA Clarification states that "HDB does not price new flats to recover the cost of land and construction.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Instead, it prices flats significantly below market value using generous subsidies to ensure they are affordable to Singaporeans." This is indisputable, for the reasons I have just explained.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is also confirmed by the fact that the vast majority of first-timer families are able to buy new BTO flats in non-mature estates and service their monthly mortgage instalments using their CPF, with zero or minimal cash outlay.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As a result, HDB incurs a net deficit in the development and sale of new flats.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Can I just check before I respond to that?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, I am just seeking to understand, so that I can give an appropriate answer.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: What is the correlation between the POFMA Correction Directions and your request?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, the subsidy is applied by HDB and that is why flats can be sold at an affordable price.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I am not sure I understand the correlation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think everybody knows that HDB applies subsidies, significant subsidies.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If Mr Singh was just asking, "Can you provide the breakdown?" – that I understand.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But he is saying in view of the POFMA Correction Directions, whether HDB will provide the breakdown.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, I will answer Mr Singh's question on whether we will provide breakdown.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I am just trying to understand how it is correlated.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Because the fact that we provided subsidies has always been known, long before the POFMA Correction Directions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, I just want to know the connection.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Again, I will answer the question, but I want to deal with the first part.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If Mr Singh says how come somebody who was an ex-economist of — did you name the organisation?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I do not think there is any rule in the law books, which says that economists and ex-economists of GIC cannot be POFMA-ed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: What the law says is that if you say something which is factually incorrect, then you are required to post a Notice, pointing out to it.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And you can challenge that if you wish to – which he has not.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Point number two is, Mr Singh still has not really answered what the correlation is, but now I will just cut to the chase, unless Mr Singh wishes to provide a further clarification.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It also said that it was "an accounting sleight of hand being the omission that the government acquired most of the land at minimal or much lower cost by compulsory acquisition" and that the "true cost price should be the original book value".

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And in response, the POFMA Clarification pointed out that actually there is a real loss.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Total development cost is land costs plus construction costs and that gives you total development cost.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The selling price is the market value of the land after it has been built, we apply a market subsidy, we derive the selling price, we put in various grants and we arrive at the effective selling price.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: [Please refer to “Clarification by the Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development”, Official Report, 7 November 2022, Vol 73, Issue No 95, Clarification section.] The effective selling price – what we sell to Singaporeans – less the total development cost, will give you, in virtually all cases, a net loss – obviously, because we are subsidising and selling below market value.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If we were to sell at market value, all purchasers of HDB BTOs will be paying a lot more.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And that is just evident, as I had explained in my earlier answer, from the resale prices after the MOP expires when they sell.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, I just wanted to establish that the POFMA Clarification talked about the net loss for a particular project.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That is a subset of the information which is already in HDB's financial statements, which is the total aggregate net loss.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And it is a separate issue from total development costs, which is a separate thing.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, when Mr Pritam Singh asked in view of the POFMA Correction Directions, is HDB going to give the breakdown of total development costs, there is not a real correlation there, as they are two separate things.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And the reason is this: what is the real important thing to Singaporeans?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The real important thing is, are you able to afford the flat?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And what the Government considers is the market value, which people will know.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In any particular area, you ask any valuer, and they will be able to give you a general value.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And you look at the selling price and the grants.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Every Singaporean who buys a BTO knows that actually the price that they are paying is less than what you would have to pay if you were paying at pure market price.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And then, what happens is, at the end of the day, for almost all cases, we have a net loss.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, different places will have different prices and different subsidies.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Singh's question was, he said, would we provide a breakdown of the cost of all new flats henceforth.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is not meaningful, because you would just be comparing this one with this one and prices in one area may not be the same as the other.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And I will do this by way of two supplementary questions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I will come back to Question Nos 3 and 4 in a while.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Since the introduction of the Prime Location Housing, or PLH, flats last year, it provides an example of why a detailed publication of HDB subsidies are actually warranted.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Another reason I would suggest to the Minister to publish the dollar value of the subsidy is to scrutinise and track the amount of subsidies being diverted for homeownership purposes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: This is, particularly, in view of the MND's 2011 decision to delink BTO prices from the rising resale market then.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Increasing the size of the subsidies under the current HDB policy would appear to be the main way through which BTO prices will be kept affordable.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In view of these new reasons, what is preventing HDB from publishing the dollar value of HDB subsidies for new BTO flats?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The second supplementary question: HDB's index for affordability – the Minister spoke about it in her last reply – only covers non-mature estates.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Why does the Ministry not disclose the corresponding affordability figures for HDB estates which are mature estates.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In respect to Prime Location Housing, it actually does not really change my answer.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Because at the end of the day, the question is – what is affordable to the person who is buying?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And we have made no secret of the fact that, for Prime Location Housing, you would have to have a greater subsidy.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It comes back to the same question, which is: why would you have to disclose or put out the development cost of every single project?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The key thing is, to the buyer, is this affordable and that is what HDB does.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And, I think, for the second question, if Mr Singh could just pinpoint the gravamen of what he is asking, so that I can be sure I address it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Sorry, is Minister referring to the second supplementary question or the second limb of the first supplementary question?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The second supplementary question pertains to disclosing the affordability index for mature estates.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But the Minister did not answer the second limb of the first supplementary question.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, the second limb, the Minister replied for PLH.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I take Minister's answer, even though I disagree with it, of course.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The second question was with regard to the delinking of BTO prices as a reason to reveal the subsidy in full.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I do have the question and I thank Mr Singh for it.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Can I ask Mr Singh to file a separate Parliamentary Question on this?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I have an answer formulated, but I also want to be sure it is accurate, and because, as you know, it affects property prices and the way people approach it.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, I think that it would be safer if it is filed and I give you an accurate answer.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, just to be clear, the question the Minister is asking me to file another question for, is the reasons why HDB does not publish the affordability index for mature BTO estates?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: For the first question, I restate my position that because we have now delinked BTO prices, the value of the subsidy becomes more important, particularly, with resale prices going up.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: On the earlier question, which I believe was directed at Mr Leong Mun Wai's Questions Nos 3 and 4, just for clarification and my understanding about how land is booked in the reserves, and I am looking at this from the perspective of reclaimed land: Singapore's total land area has grown by 2.45 square kilometres per year for 60 years – from 851 square kilometres in 1962 to 728 square kilometres in 2020.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The state can reclaim land and draw on the reserves for land reclamation activities and expenses – I think Minister also alluded to that in her reply.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The second one is, for land that has been reclaimed years prior, is the revaluation for marking to market done once a year based on the annual LBC rates, or once every six months based on the six-monthly LBC rates, or is the value of the land in past reserves held at the cost of land reclamation until it is sold to the Government for specific use?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Again, Sir, I would ask Mr Singh to file a Parliamentary Question formally.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The answer is likely to be technical, it has to do with how we treat the land in our books and I really want to make sure that both the Accountant-General and the Auditor-General are satisfied that what I say is not inaccurate.
